<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Critical reading: Achterberg et al., systematic review and meta-analysis

This is the most balanced of the four documents. It pre-registered its protocol, separated the per-hour and per-worker outcomes, tested the moderators that the earlier critiques identified, and rejected both "sector-general" and "entirely an artifact." Its central conclusion, a real per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% with per-worker output falling in coverage-bound work, is well supported.

The weak points are:
- the duration and novelty claim, which repeats the overreach it criticises in others;
- the reading of the small-study analysis;
- some ambiguity about how the multi-setting studies were coded;
- the lack of a "best evidence" subgroup that would directly answer Varga & Holm.

## Arithmetic and internal consistency

The study counts add up: 9 + 14, 8 + 15, 13 + 7 + 3 and 12 + 11 all equal 23.

The paired per-hour and per-worker estimates imply a fall in hours in each subgroup (implied hours ratio = per-worker ratio ÷ per-hour ratio). They were pooled separately, so this is only approximate:

| Subgroup | Implied hours change |
|---|---|
| All | −13% |
| Controlled | −11% |
| Uncontrolled | −16% |
| Actual hours | −11% |
| Scheduled hours | −15% |
| Coverage-bound | −14% |

These are coherent. They also make a point the review doesn't draw out: studies measuring actual hours show a cut of only about 11%, consistent with Varden and with the Halden re-analysis.

The comparison between uncontrolled and controlled designs on **per-worker** output is telling and also under-discussed: −0.2% for uncontrolled versus −4.1% for controlled. Before–after designs appear to hide a real per-worker loss, not just inflate the per-hour figure.

## 1. The duration claim overreaches

> "Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside."

This repeats in the abstract and does not follow:

- **There are only four studies.** Their CI (+6.2% to +22.4%) runs from the controlled estimate to well above the uncontrolled one. That is too wide to show the absence of decay.
- **This is a between-study comparison.** Decay is a within-study question. The right test is the trajectory over time inside each study, for example Halden's monthly index or Varden at 9 and 24 months.
- **Survivorship.** Follow-up past 12 months mostly exists where a scheme *continued*, and schemes continue because they worked. Long-follow-up studies are pre-selected for persistence.
- **No like-for-like comparison.** If the four long studies are mostly uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, they should be compared with the +18.7% or +16.6% subgroups, not the +13.4% overall figure. Against those, +14.0% could actually *indicate* decay. The review doesn't report the designs of the four.

The defensible claim is "no evidence of decay in the few long studies; durability remains largely untested." Varga & Holm overreached in claiming novelty explains everything. This review overreaches in the opposite direction by dismissing it.

## 2. The small-study analysis is probably confounded with the moderators

Egger's test and trim-and-fill are unreliable under high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Here the heterogeneity has a known structure: small studies are plausibly the uncontrolled, scheduled-hours, manager-reported pilots.

The funnel asymmetry may therefore reflect **design differences**, not publication bias. The interpretation that "small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published" is one explanation among several. Two consequences:

- **Better analyses were available.** Egger's test should be run with the moderators included, or a selection model used. Otherwise the publication-bias claim is untested.
- **The convergence is partly circular.** The Discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies *and* the bias-adjusted estimate "converge" on 8–10%. If small-study asymmetry is driven by design, these are largely the same correction seen four ways, not independent confirmation.

## 3. The review doesn't answer Varga & Holm directly

The review rejects the "entirely an artifact" claim because the controlled and actual-hours subgroups exclude zero. But each subgroup avoids only some of the problems:

- **Controlled studies** may still use scheduled hours and manager-reported output.
- **Actual-hours studies** may be uncontrolled.

The decisive analysis is the **intersection**: controlled, actual hours and record-based output. Varden's case-processing stratum is one such study (+12.5%, CI +6.9 to +18.4). The review should report how many such studies there are and what they show. If even two or three point the same way, the rebuttal is much stronger than any single-moderator subgroup.

The review's conclusion is probably right. The analysis offered doesn't fully demonstrate it.

## 4. How the multi-setting studies were coded

- **Varden** has a discretionary stratum and a coverage-bound stratum with opposite per-worker results. Was it coded "mixed," split into two entries, or placed in one category? If it was coded mixed, the clearest randomised evidence on work type is lost from the moderator analysis. If it was split, then k = 23 counts effect sizes, not studies, and those need a multilevel model.
- **Halden** spans six sectors and has the same problem.
- **Which Halden estimates were used?** The original working paper reports scheduled hours and manager output. The re-analysis supplies actual hours and record-based output for subsets. The methods say actual hours were used "where a study reported" them, so it's unclear whether the re-analysis figures were used. Halden's attrition, which the original paper misreported, also isn't mentioned.

## 5. Size of the hours cut is not a moderator

Inclusion requires a cut of at least 10%, and cuts vary. Per-hour gains are mechanically larger for larger cuts when output stays roughly constant. A 10% cut with flat output gives +11%; a 20% cut gives +25%.

Without the size of the hours reduction as a moderator, part of the heterogeneity, and possibly part of the work-type and design effects, is just variation in how much hours were cut. This is the same metric artefact all three earlier documents struggled with.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Coverage-bound per-hour gain (+6.2%).** The review calls this "real." As in Varden, much of it plausibly reflects higher utilisation, with less idle time and longer queues, not greater efficiency. The per-worker result (−8.9%, I² = 22%) is the more meaningful and better-supported finding.
- **Meta-regression capacity.** k = 23 with three correlated moderators, one of them with three levels, means "58% of variance explained" is unstable. The authors acknowledge this.
- **Fatigue as a mechanism.** r = 0.18 across 11 studies is an ecological, low-power correlation over heterogeneous fatigue scales. It weakly argues against fatigue as the main driver but can't rule out a within-study effect. The paper reads it about right.
- **Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it.** This is vote-counting, and studies tend to report favourable secondary outcomes. The pooled −31% is consistent with Varden (−29%) and is plausibly robust, but the selective-reporting caveat belongs here.
- **Search.** Contacting "authors of known pilots" favours publicised pilots. That is relevant given the small-study finding.
- **No prediction interval for per-worker output.** Given I² = 74%, one should be reported, since per-worker output is the outcome that matters for policy.

## How the four documents fit together

| Question | Halden | Varden | Varga & Holm | Meta-analysis | Best current reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain | +23% | +12.5% (discretionary) | about +11%, "artifact" | +8 to 10% (rigorous subsets) | Real, about 8–12%, roughly half the headline |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | about 0% | −2% (n.s.) | — | +0.6% overall, −2.7% controlled | Roughly maintained, possibly a small loss |
| Coverage-bound work | "Sector-general" | −11%, worse service | −11% | −9%, consistent | Output falls unless staff are added |
| Durability | 6 months | 9 months | Novelty likely | "No decay" | Untested; within-study long follow-up is needed |
| Mechanism | Fatigue | Meetings (exploratory) | Rejects both | Fatigue weak; meetings unassessed | Unknown |
| Sick leave | −36% | −29% | — | −31% | Robust reduction |

## Bottom line

The review gets the main picture right:
- per-hour gains are real but about half the headline figures;
- per-worker output holds roughly steady in discretionary work and falls in coverage-bound work;
- design and measurement explain much of the earlier optimism.

It should:
1. drop or heavily qualify the claim that novelty "can be set aside";
2. reanalyse small-study effects conditional on the moderators;
3. report the controlled + actual-hours + record-based intersection;
4. clarify how Varden and Halden were coded and which Halden estimates were used;
5. add the size of the hours cut as a moderator.

Durability and mechanism remain the two open questions. The best near-term evidence will be Varden's 24-month follow-up, including its registered test of the meetings hypothesis.
